You replace the object with a pronoun (le, la, les, l’) so you don’t repeat yourself, in the present, past and future.
“Je le vois” = I see him / it
“Tu me vois ?” = can you see me?
je connais, nous connaissons; participle: connu

To use direct object pronouns: le, la, l’, les, me, te, nous, vous.
To put the pronoun in the right place: before the verb (je la vois).
To use it in the passé composé (je l’ai vue) and with an infinitive (je vais la chercher).
To conjugate CONNAÎTRE and tell it apart from SAVOIR.
To introduce someone and talk about a first meeting.
February. Elena, Ioana’s mother, is coming to Lyon for the first time, for a week. Ioana is at the airport with Julien, who is very nervous: he’s about to meet his “mother-in-law”.
Can you see your mother? There are a lot of people.
No, I can’t see her yet… Wait! Yes, I can see her! The lady in the red coat!
She looks nice. And the presents, have you got them?
Yes, I’ve got them in my bag. Mum! Mum, over here!
Ioana, darling! Come here, let me look at you. You’ve lost weight, haven’t you?
Oh no, Mum! I eat very well here. Mum, this is Julien.
Hello, madam. Nice to meet you. I’m very happy to meet you.
Nice to meet you, Julien. Ioana talks about you a lot! I already know you a little.
Really? I hope she says nice things! Your suitcase, I’ll take it.
Thank you, you’re very kind. Careful, it’s heavy. I’ve brought cozonac, țuică and jams for you!
Mum! You put all that in the suitcase?
Of course! I spent three days packing it. And luckily customs didn’t open it.
No, I don’t know it. But I’ve seen photos. You’re going to show it to me, aren’t you?
With pleasure! Tomorrow I’ll take you to Fourvière. And tonight I’m taking you out to a restaurant.
(to Ioana, in Romanian) He’s polite, your Julien. I like him.
go (“vous allez montrer” = you’re going to show)
like him (“je l’aime bien” = I like him)
“Je le vois” = “zhuhl VWA”, “je la vois” = “zhuh la VWA”. Le is weak and almost disappears; la is heard clearly.
“Je les aime” = “zhuh lay-ZEM”, with a z liaison. “Je les ai” = “zhuh lay-ZAY”.
“Je l’ai vu” (I saw him) = “zhuh lay VU”, “je les ai vus” (I saw them) = “zhuh lay-zay VU”. The only difference is the linking z!
Je connais = “zhuh ko-NEH”, nous connaissons = “noo ko-neh-SÕ”. The circumflex on î doesn’t change the sound.
“Si” as an answer = “yes (actually)”, after a negative question: “Tu ne la vois pas ? — Si !” Say it short and firm.
To avoid repeating a noun, you replace it with a pronoun, just like English: “I see the suitcase → I see it”. In French:
Before a vowel: me, te, le, la become m’, t’, l’: “Je l’aime” (I love him / her), “Tu m’aides ?” (Will you help me?).
Don’t confuse “le, la, les” as pronouns (before a VERB) and “le, la, les” as articles (before a NOUN). “Je prends la valise” → “Je la prends”.
2. Where the pronoun goes: before the verb
Unlike English (“I see it”), the pronoun comes BEFORE the conjugated verb:
I know Lyon. → I know it.
Have you got the presents? → Have you got them?
With a negation: ne + pronoun + verb + pas.
With an infinitive (aller, vouloir, pouvoir + infinitive), the pronoun goes before the INFINITIVE:
I’m going to pick her up at the airport.
I want to look at you.
Wrong: “Je la vais chercher”. Correct: “Je vais la chercher”. The pronoun sticks to the verb it belongs to (chercher).
3. In the passé composé: before the auxiliary, with agreement
In the passé composé, the pronoun goes before the auxiliary (avoir):
And a new rule: when the direct object pronoun comes BEFORE avoir, the participle agrees with it (+e for feminine, +s for plural):
Je les ai mises dans la valise.

The agreement usually only shows in writing (préparé / préparée sound the same). Exception: participles ending in a consonant: “mis / mise”, “pris / prise”, “ouvert / ouverte” sound different. Elena says: “la douane ne l’a pas ouverte”.
English has one verb, “to know”. French splits it clearly:
Je connais Julien. Je connais Lyon.
information, facts, knowing how to do something (+ verb, que, où, si…)
Je sais nager. Je sais où il habite.
“Je sais Lyon” is wrong. For a place or a person: “Je connais Lyon”. And the other way round: “Je connais nager” is wrong; correct: “Je sais nager”.
Madame, je vous présente mon collègue, Karim.
On m’a beaucoup parlé de vous !
Je suis très content(e) de vous rencontrer.
“La belle-mère” = mother-in-law (and stepmother), “le beau-père” = father-in-law (and stepfather), “le gendre” = son-in-law, “la belle-fille” = daughter-in-law. All in-laws get “beau / belle”.
Can you see Ioana? — Yes, I can see her.
Have you got the tickets? — Yes, I’ve got them.
I’m going to pick her up.
The pronoun goes before the verb.
knowing how to do something → savoir
I put them in the car.
Elena porte un manteau de quelle couleur ?
Du cozonac, de la țuică et des confitures
Non, elle ne le connaît pas
I already know you a little.
He’s polite, your Julien. I like him.
Elena liked Julien. But she was a Romanian mother, and a Romanian mother always tests her future son-in-law.
On Tuesday she decided to do the first test: cooking. She made sarmale and served them to Julien.
Julien tasted them. Then he ate them all. He even asked for more. First test: passed!
On Wednesday, second test: patience. Elena wanted to visit every museum in Lyon. Julien went with her everywhere, without complaining.
At the Confluences museum she stopped in front of every object. Julien waited for her, smiling. They stayed there four hours.
“Aren’t you tired?” Elena asked him. “No, madam. I love museums,” lied Julien, very politely.
On Thursday, the third and hardest test: the țuică. Elena took a bottle out of her suitcase. “At home we drink it on big occasions.”
She filled two little glasses. Julien took his, looked at it, then drank it in one go.
He went bright red. He coughed. His eyes were watering. But he said: “Delicious! Noroc!”
Elena laughed for five minutes. So did Ioana. Even Victor, watching them from the balcony, seemed to laugh.
On Friday, at the airport, Elena hugged Julien. “Julien, I’ll expect you in Iași this summer. My husband wants to meet you.”
Then she added, smiling: “And he has a lot of țuică.”
In the car Julien was a little pale. “Ioana, your father… does he drink it often, the țuică?” Ioana looked at him and smiled. She didn’t answer.
to complain (“sans se plaindre” = without complaining)

Elena writes in the evening, in French (she’s practising too!). Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions.
Monday evening. I arrived in Lyon this morning. Ioana was waiting for me at the airport with Julien.
I found her in good shape. She hasn’t lost weight after all. She’s even put on a little!
Julien, I find him very kind. He carried my suitcase all the way to the car. It weighed twenty-three kilos!
He speaks a little Romanian. He’s learnt three words: “bună ziua”, “mulțumesc” and “cozonac”. I congratulated him.
Tonight he took us to a Lyon bouchon. I ate quenelles. I found them delicious.
I met Ioana’s neighbour, Madame Bernard. I already knew her from my daughter’s stories.
She has a very fat cat, Victor. He stared at me for a long time, then he ate a piece of my cozonac!
Ioana is happy here, I can see it. I’m proud of her.
But I’m going to ask her an important question: when is she going to introduce Julien to us officially, in Iași?
find (“je le trouve gentil” = I find him kind)
go (“je vais poser” = I’m going to ask)
Julien connaît combien de mots roumains ?
